artist_name: Benjamin Smith II & James Smith III
artwork_title: A set of four George III silver sauce tureens
provenance: These are the arms of HOWARD, and with the addition of the Earls Coronet finial, it is likely these arms relate to of Richard HOWARD (1748-1816) 4th Earl of Effingham and 10th Baron of Effingham. He was the second son of Thomas Howard, 2nd Earl of Effingham, and Elizabeth Beckford, he was educated at Eton College from 1755 to 1762 before commissioning as a Lieutenant in the 1st Horse Guards, serving from 1768 until 1771. He then entered politics, Howard represented Steyning in the House of Commons from 1784 to 1790. Upon the death of his brother Thomas in 1791 without male issue, Howard succeeded as 4th Earl and 10th Baron Howard of Effingham, transferring his parliamentary service to the House of Lords, he married Harriet Elizabeth Marsh in 1785. He held court positions as Secretary and Comptroller to Queen Charlotte from 1784 to 1814, advancing to Treasurer until 1816, roles that showed his close ties to the royal household amid the later years of George III's reign.

description_block:
Triptych Icon with the Three Hierarchs, Feasts of the Liturgical Year, the Prophet Elijah, Saints Kosmas and Damian, and Saint Catherine

Cretan School, second half of the 17th century
traditionally painted in strong colours on a gilt ground, with ornate Baroque-inspired cresting, the central exterior panel depicts the Three Holy Hierarchs Basil the Great, John Chrysostom, and Gregory of Nazianzus, represented frontally and holding Gospel books, the interior is organized as a complex devotional and liturgical program. The central compartment contains scenes from the Dodekaorton and the Passion cycle, including the Baptism of Christ, the Raising of Lazarus, the Entry into Jerusalem, the Crucifixion, the Anastasis, the Myrrhbearers at the Tomb, the Ascension, and the Transfiguration. Left wing presents episodes from the life of Elijah within a mountainous wilderness landscape, together with the Annunciation and other prophetic prefigurations, while the opposite wing includes an icon of Catherine of Alexandria, traditionally painted in strong colours, the saint enthroned with her attributes, with Holy Unmercenary Saints Cosmas and Damian on verso of Elijah
 open: 41 x 55 cm (16 1/8 x 55 in); closed: 41 x 20 cm (16 1/8 x 7 7/8 in).

artwork_title: A rare and important set of four English carved oak heraldic newel post finial beasts representing the royal arms
provenance: Formerly surmounting the staircase at Beachampton Farm, North East of Buckingham. Sold in a London auction room, possibly in the 1970s or 1980s. A Dutch private collection. Thence by descent. Beachampton Hall, (formerly known as Hall Farmhouse) was originally built in the late 15th century. It was owned by Catherine Parr, and formed part of her extensive dowry when she married King Henry VIII. It was then heavily altered at the beginning of the 16th century by the Pigot family with the great chamber likely to have been rebuilt by Sir Thomas Pigot between 1603-1611. This was possibly for the reception of Queen Anne of Denmark and her court that visited in July 1603, when the gardens were also installed. Residents of the Hall include the Marquess of Salisbury, the Cecil family and a former Lord Mayor London. The elaborate carved staircase, which the present lot was part of, was largely removed in 1922.
